results.description: Influence of Cutting Schedule Scheduling irrigations of alfalfa is complicated by the harvest schedule, which occurs about every 28 to 30 days in most areas. The first irrigation after harvest cannot occur until the alfalfa bales are removed. The final irrigation between harvests will need to occur at a time that provides sufficient soil drying before the harvest. Thus, irrigation scheduling of alfalfa is often controlled by the harvest schedule, not by allowable soil mois­ ture depletion. [...] Irrigate before the yield is reduced by insuf­ ficient soil moisture. This requires irrigating frequently enough to prevent excessive soil moisture depletion. A standard approach to irrigation scheduling (called the water balance or checkbook method) is to determine how much soil moisture can be depleted between irrigations without reducing crop yield, then irrigate when total alfalfa ET between irriga­ tions equals that depletion. results.description:
Water budgeting approaches or “checkbook scheduling” involves monitoring soil moisture in addition to determining daily crop water use through evapotranspiration (ET). Soil moisture can be monitored using moisture-sensing instrumentation. With alfalfa, irrigation typically begins with only about 50% depletion of available water in the root zone. See more about irrigation scheduling in Minnesota at: [...] Other irrigation scheduling considerations unique to alfalfa include: 1) avoid scheduling during times of peak ET in the summer months, 2) avoid irrigation 1 week before harvest to facilitate harvest equipment and to avoid compaction, 3) irrigate immediately after a harvest, and 4) avoid irrigation when alfalfa is undergoing the dormancy reaction in the fall. [...] The growth stage at which alfalfa can tolerate extended soil moisture deficits has not been established, but by 8 weeks, the risk of drought damage is minimized as plants have a well-developed crown and multiple stems.

requirements.missing: No document provides an explicit soil moisture threshold (e.g., volumetric water content % or matric potential kPa) that triggers post-cutting irrigation for alfalfa regrowth. S12 gives ET rates and seasonal water use (0.30 in/day growing season → 0.10 in/day fall; ~5-6 in/cutting) with recommendation to 'use ET measurement gages or soil moisture monitoring,' but no numeric soil-moisture trigger or volume-to-apply criterion tied to regrowth phase is specified.

No document provides regrowth-stage nutrient removal rates (N, P, K) with quantified rates per ton or per regrowth interval for alfalfa (Medicago sativa). S15 gives removal per ton (K₂O 55 lb, P₂O₅ 12 lb, S 4-6 lb) and Utah soil-test-based P/K recommendations, but these are general stand fertilization tables, not tied to regrowth stage or regrowth yield potential. S14 gives grass N split-rate (40 lb N/cutting) but explicitly states N is seldom beneficial on established alfalfa. S13 gives N/P/K trial rates in kg ha⁻¹ for North China Plain plots but is a multi-year fertilizer-combination experiment, not a regrowth-specific removal/recommendation.

No document supplies actual field measurements with original units (mm, kg/ha, cm soil moisture, days) together with explicit geography/cropping system for the post-cutting regrowth irrigation decision question. S12 references Becker and St. Paul MN precipitation/temperature and ET rates in inches/day with explicit geography, but these are climate/yield-trial observations, not regrowth-irrigation-management measurements. S13 is in kg ha⁻¹ at 38°08′N 117°51′E North China Plain, but addresses long-term NPK balance rather than post-cut regrowth irrigation scheduling.
